## 1. Purpose

This module compares three genomic best linear unbiased prediction
(GBLUP) structures from [R04A](real_data_gblup.html) and four
artificial neural-network (ANN) variants from
[R04B](real_data_ann.html). All seven methods predict the same
precomputed individual phenotypic BLUPs using the common outer
cross-validation design established in
[R03](real_data_validation.html). The stored results are read directly;
no genomic prediction model is refitted in this module.

| Model | Genomic structure or explicit weight penalty |
|:------|:---------------------------------------------|
| GBLUP_A | Additive genomic relationship |
| GBLUP_AD | Additive and dominance genomic relationships |
| GBLUP_ADE | Additive, dominance and additive-by-additive epistatic genomic relationships |
| ANN_0 | No explicit L1 or L2 penalty |
| ANN_L1 | L1 weight penalty |
| ANN_L2 | L2 weight penalty |
| ANN_L1_L2 | Simultaneous L1 and L2 weight penalties |

All four ANN variants use early stopping during the selection of
training duration. ANN_0 therefore denotes the absence of explicit
L1 and L2 penalties, not the absence of every form of regularization.
The GBLUP structures use their respective genomic relationship matrices,
whereas the ANN variants use genomic markers as network inputs.

The population comprises 195 individuals evaluated for Cer, BM and LP.
Five repetitions of five-fold outer cross-validation yield 25
assessment splits per trait and model, each with 39 held-out individuals.
The ANN hyperparameters were selected within the corresponding outer
analysis samples in R04B; GBLUP uses the three prespecified structures
in R04A.

Unlike the simulated analysis, the real data do not provide known true
genetic values. The evaluation target is the phenotypic BLUP, which was
estimated before the genomic validation design and was not refitted
within each genomic split. Agreement with these BLUPs therefore measures
genomic prediction of the available phenotypic reference, not accuracy
against known true genetic values. Throughout this module, GEBV denotes
the stored genomic prediction on the BLUP scale; it does not imply
that the full prediction is an additive breeding value for every model.

The comparison distinguishes three scientific questions:

- How well does each model predict the phenotypic BLUP within an outer
  assessment split? Pearson, Spearman, RMSE and MAE are the primary
  metrics; bias and calibration slope provide complementary information.
- How do the models differ on matched outer splits?
- How well do the mean out-of-fold (OOF) predictions recover individual
  rankings and the upper 20% of the phenotypic BLUP distribution, and
  how similar are the ranking strata produced by different models?

Repeated cross-validation reuses individuals across analysis sets and
assessment repetitions. The split-level summaries and contrasts are
descriptive, not significance tests based on 25 independent replicates.

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  cache = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center",
  out.width = "100%"
)

COMPARISON_DIR <- "output/real/comparison"

FIGURE_DIR <- file.path(COMPARISON_DIR, "figures")

dir.create(COMPARISON_DIR, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

dir.create(FIGURE_DIR, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

## 2. Prediction data and cross-validation

### 2.1 Packages and dependencies

The module uses `knitr` and `kableExtra` for tables and `ggplot2` with
`ggthemes` for figures. The stored fitting outputs are sufficient for
the comparison; neither BGLR nor torch is required here.

```{r packages}
library(knitr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggthemes)
```

### 2.2 Saved prediction results and validation design

The six fitting outputs have three different units of observation.
The validation design from R03 supplies the assessment identifiers
against which their coverage is examined.

| Input object | Unit of observation | Expected rows |
|:-------------|:--------------------|--------------:|
| gblup_results | Trait, outer split and GBLUP structure | 225 |
| ann_results | Trait, outer split and ANN variant | 300 |
| gblup_predictions | Held-out individual, trait, outer split and GBLUP structure | 8,775 |
| ann_predictions | Held-out individual, trait, outer split and ANN variant | 11,700 |
| gblup_ranking | Individual, trait and GBLUP structure | 1,755 |
| ann_ranking | Individual, trait and ANN variant | 2,340 |

```{r read-model-predictions}
gblup_results <- readRDS("output/real/gblup/real_gblup_results.rds")

gblup_predictions <- readRDS("output/real/gblup/real_gblup_predictions.rds")

gblup_ranking <- readRDS("output/real/gblup/real_gblup_individual_ranking.rds")

ann_results <- readRDS("output/real/ann/final/real_ann_results.rds")

ann_predictions <- readRDS("output/real/ann/final/real_ann_predictions.rds")

ann_ranking <- readRDS("output/real/ann/final/real_ann_individual_ranking.rds")
```

The common validation object is read without regenerating folds.

```{r comparison-validation-design}
comparison_cv <- readRDS("output/real/validation/real_cv_design.rds")

comparison_assessment <- comparison_cv$outer_assignments[
  , c("Repetition", "OuterFold", "SplitID", "ID"), drop = FALSE
]
names(comparison_assessment)[
  names(comparison_assessment) == "OuterFold"
] <- "Fold"
```

### 2.3 Harmonizing the result columns and model identifiers

Both fitting modules use the same metrics and prediction targets.
The following named vectors map the original column names to the
short names used throughout this comparison. A loop applies each
mapping to the corresponding pair of data frames. Only column names
change; the stored values, row order and files remain unchanged.

```{r normalize-comparison-columns}
metric_names <- c(
  BLUP_Correlation = "Pearson", BLUP_Spearman = "Spearman",
  BLUP_RMSE = "RMSE", BLUP_MAE = "MAE",
  BLUP_Bias = "Bias", BLUP_Slope = "Slope"
)
prediction_names <- c(Observed_BLUP = "BLUP", Predicted_BLUP = "GEBV")
ranking_names <- c(
  prediction_names, Prediction_SD = "GEBV_SD",
  Observed_Rank = "BLUP_Rank", Predicted_Rank = "GEBV_Rank",
  Observed_Top20 = "BLUP_Top20", Predicted_Top20 = "GEBV_Top20"
)

# Harmonize the metric, prediction and ranking columns separately.
for (old_name in names(metric_names)) {
  names(gblup_results)[names(gblup_results) == old_name] <- metric_names[[old_name]]
  names(ann_results)[names(ann_results) == old_name] <- metric_names[[old_name]]
}

for (old_name in names(prediction_names)) {
  names(gblup_predictions)[names(gblup_predictions) == old_name] <- prediction_names[[old_name]]
  names(ann_predictions)[names(ann_predictions) == old_name] <- prediction_names[[old_name]]
}

for (old_name in names(ranking_names)) {
  names(gblup_ranking)[names(gblup_ranking) == old_name] <- ranking_names[[old_name]]
  names(ann_ranking)[names(ann_ranking) == old_name] <- ranking_names[[old_name]]
}
```

The scientific identifiers select the seven existing models. The
display labels provide a common order for tables and figures;
they do not define new model structures.

```{r compared-models}
traits <- c("Cer", "BM", "LP")

gblup_models <- c("GBLUP_A", "GBLUP_AD", "GBLUP_ADE")

ann_models <- c("ANN_0", "ANN_L1", "ANN_L2", "ANN_L1_L2")

model_order <- c(gblup_models, ann_models)

model_labels <- c("GBLUP-A", "GBLUP-AD", "GBLUP-ADE", "ANN-0", "ANN-L1", "ANN-L2", "ANN-L1+L2")

```

### 2.4 Numbers of assessments and predictions

Each model contributes 75 trait-by-split results, 2,925 held-out
predictions and 585 individual OOF ranking records. The first table
counts the two families' stored results and prediction records.
The ranking table then counts the individual records separately.

```{r input-record-counts}
input_summary <- data.frame(
  Branch = c("GBLUP", "ANN"),
  Models = c(length(gblup_models), length(ann_models)),
  Model_trait_split_results = c(nrow(gblup_results), nrow(ann_results)),
  GEBV_records = c(nrow(gblup_predictions), nrow(ann_predictions)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

input_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    caption = "Cross-validation predictions and performance records by model family",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
  )
```

```{r ranking-input-counts}
ranking_input_summary <- data.frame(
  Family = c("GBLUP", "ANN"),
  Individuals_per_trait_model = length(comparison_cv$ids),
  Ranking_records = c(nrow(gblup_ranking), nrow(ann_ranking)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  ranking_input_summary, format = "html", row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Stored individual OOF ranking records",
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
)
```

The expected combined dimensions are 525 split-level results,
20,475 individual held-out predictions and 4,095 individual ranking
records. These totals describe different units of observation and
must not be interpreted as independent biological replicates.

### 2.5 Matched outer tasks and assessment individuals

Cross-model matching uses the model-independent keys
`Trait`, `Repetition`, `Fold` and `SplitID`. The individual
identifier `ID` is added when matching predictions. The original
TaskID is not used because its definition differs across the fitting
modules.

The stored R03 outer assignment table is crossed with the three
traits to obtain the expected assessment keys for one model. Its
distinct split keys define the expected result records.

```{r comparison-expected-keys}
result_keys <- c("Trait", "Repetition", "Fold", "SplitID")
comparison_keys <- c(result_keys, "ID")

expected_prediction_keys <- merge(
  data.frame(Trait = traits, stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
  comparison_assessment,
  by = NULL
)
expected_prediction_keys <- expected_prediction_keys[
  , comparison_keys, drop = FALSE
]

expected_result_keys <- unique(expected_prediction_keys[
  , result_keys, drop = FALSE
])
```

The next tables distinguish duplicate keys, absent expected records
and unexpected records. Matching is performed on distinct keys so
that duplicates cannot inflate the number of matched records.
The expected counts are 75 distinct result keys and 2,925 distinct
prediction keys per model. Duplicate, missing and unexpected counts
should all be zero.

```{r comparison-key-coverage}
result_key_coverage <- data.frame()
prediction_key_coverage <- data.frame()
assessment_coverage <- data.frame()

for (model_name in model_order) {
  if (model_name %in% gblup_models) {
    model_results <- gblup_results[gblup_results$Model == model_name, , drop = FALSE]
    model_predictions <- gblup_predictions[gblup_predictions$Model == model_name, , drop = FALSE]
  } else {
    model_results <- ann_results[ann_results$Model == model_name, , drop = FALSE]
    model_predictions <- ann_predictions[ann_predictions$Model == model_name, , drop = FALSE]
  }

  observed_result_keys <- unique(model_results[, result_keys, drop = FALSE])
  observed_prediction_keys <- unique(model_predictions[, comparison_keys, drop = FALSE])

  matched_result_keys <- merge(
    expected_result_keys, observed_result_keys, by = result_keys
  )
  matched_prediction_keys <- merge(
    expected_prediction_keys, observed_prediction_keys, by = comparison_keys
  )

  result_key_coverage <- rbind(result_key_coverage, data.frame(
    Model = model_name,
    Records = nrow(model_results),
    Distinct_keys = nrow(observed_result_keys),
    Duplicate_keys = nrow(model_results) - nrow(observed_result_keys),
    Missing_keys = nrow(expected_result_keys) - nrow(matched_result_keys),
    Unexpected_keys = nrow(observed_result_keys) - nrow(matched_result_keys),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ))

  prediction_key_coverage <- rbind(prediction_key_coverage, data.frame(
    Model = model_name,
    Records = nrow(model_predictions),
    Distinct_keys = nrow(observed_prediction_keys),
    Duplicate_keys = nrow(model_predictions) - nrow(observed_prediction_keys),
    Missing_keys = nrow(expected_prediction_keys) - nrow(matched_prediction_keys),
    Unexpected_keys = nrow(observed_prediction_keys) - nrow(matched_prediction_keys),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ))

  # Count assessment records in each trait-by-split task.
  task_sizes <- aggregate(
    list(N = rep(1L, nrow(model_predictions))),
    by = model_predictions[, result_keys, drop = FALSE], FUN = sum
  )
  # Count predictions per individual and repetition, separately by trait.
  repetition_sizes <- aggregate(
    list(N = rep(1L, nrow(model_predictions))),
    by = model_predictions[, c("Trait", "ID", "Repetition")], FUN = sum
  )
  individual_sizes <- aggregate(
    list(N = rep(1L, nrow(model_predictions))),
    by = model_predictions[, c("Trait", "ID")], FUN = sum
  )

  assessment_coverage <- rbind(assessment_coverage, data.frame(
    Model = model_name,
    Tasks = nrow(task_sizes),
    Min_assessment_N = min(task_sizes$N),
    Max_assessment_N = max(task_sizes$N),
    Trait_individuals = nrow(individual_sizes),
    Min_OOF_N = min(individual_sizes$N),
    Max_OOF_N = max(individual_sizes$N),
    Repetition_groups = nrow(repetition_sizes),
    Non_single_repetition_groups = sum(repetition_sizes$N != 1L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ))
}

knitr::kable(
  result_key_coverage, format = "html", row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Result-key coverage relative to the R03 design",
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
)
```

```{r display-prediction-key-coverage}
knitr::kable(
  prediction_key_coverage, format = "html", row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Individual assessment-key coverage relative to the R03 design",
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
)
```

The coverage counts should be read together with the next table:
each model should have 75 tasks of 39 predictions, 585
trait-individual groups with five OOF predictions each, and 2,925
trait-individual-repetition groups with one prediction each.
The key comparisons above also account for missing groups, which
cannot be identified from observed group sizes alone.

```{r display-assessment-coverage}
knitr::kable(
  assessment_coverage, format = "html", row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Assessment sample sizes and repeated OOF prediction coverage",
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "100%")
```

### 2.6 Matched BLUP targets across models

GBLUP-A is used only as a reference for checking the equality of
phenotypic BLUP targets, not as a preferred prediction method.
After matching on the individual assessment keys, the maximum
absolute BLUP difference measures target agreement. Full agreement
requires complete, unique keys (Section 2.5), finite targets and
zero difference for every matched record.

```{r matched-blup-targets}
comparison_keys <- c("Trait", "Repetition", "Fold", "SplitID", "ID")

blup_check <- gblup_predictions[
  gblup_predictions$Model == "GBLUP_A",
  c(comparison_keys, "BLUP"),
  drop = FALSE
]

target_match <- data.frame(
  Model = character(0),
  Matched_records = integer(0),
  Maximum_BLUP_difference = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (model_name in model_order) {

  if (model_name %in% gblup_models) {

    model_predictions <- gblup_predictions[
      gblup_predictions$Model == model_name,
      c(comparison_keys, "BLUP"),
      drop = FALSE
    ]

  } else {

    model_predictions <- ann_predictions[
      ann_predictions$Model == model_name,
      c(comparison_keys, "BLUP"),
      drop = FALSE
    ]
  }

  matched <- merge(
    blup_check,
    model_predictions,
    by = comparison_keys,
    suffixes = c("_Check", "_Model"),
    all = FALSE,
    sort = FALSE
  )

  maximum_difference <- max(abs(matched$BLUP_Check - matched$BLUP_Model))

  target_match <- rbind(
    target_match,
    data.frame(
      Model = model_name,
      Matched_records = nrow(matched),
      Maximum_BLUP_difference = maximum_difference,
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  )
}

```

```{r display-blup-alignment}
target_match$Model <- factor(target_match$Model, levels = model_order, labels = model_labels)

target_match |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    digits = 12,
    caption = "BLUP alignment across the seven genomic models",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
  )
```

The target-alignment table reports the number of matched records
and the maximum difference. Its values must be interpreted alongside
the key-coverage tables rather than as evidence of completeness
from an inner join alone.

## 3. Evaluation metrics

### 3.1 Association and prediction error within an outer split

Let \(y_i\) denote the phenotypic BLUP and \(\widehat y_i\) the
stored genomic prediction for held-out individual \(i\). Each
assessment split contains \(n=39\) individuals.

| Metric | Interpretation | Reference direction |
|:-------|:---------------|:--------------------|
| Pearson | Linear association | Higher |
| Spearman | Rank association | Higher |
| RMSE | Quadratic prediction error | Lower |
| MAE | Absolute prediction error | Lower |
| Bias | Mean signed prediction error | Near zero |
| Slope | Calibration of predicted scale | Near one |

Pearson correlation measures linear association:

\[
r=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\bar y)(\widehat y_i-\overline{\widehat y})}
{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\bar y)^2
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\widehat y_i-\overline{\widehat y})^2}}.
\]

Spearman correlation is Pearson correlation applied to the ranks
of observed and predicted values, using average ranks for ties.
A high correlation does not establish equality of predictions and
targets or absence of systematic error.

The error metrics on the original BLUP scale are

\[
\operatorname{RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\widehat y_i-y_i)^2},
\qquad
\operatorname{MAE}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\widehat y_i-y_i|.
\]

RMSE gives larger errors greater weight than MAE. Both are expressed
on the scale of the trait, so error magnitudes should be compared
within traits, not pooled across traits with different scales.

The stored fitting procedures return undefined correlations when
observed or predicted values are constant. Finite RMSE and MAE
remain meaningful in these cases. Section 4 distinguishes the
model-specific available splits from the common finite splits
used in direct correlation comparisons.

### 3.2 Complementary calibration metrics

Mean signed prediction error is defined as

\[
\operatorname{Bias}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\widehat y_i-y_i).
\]

Positive bias indicates average overprediction; negative bias
indicates underprediction. Bias near zero can result from
cancellation of positive and negative errors.

The calibration slope is the prediction coefficient in a regression
with an intercept:

\[
y_i=\alpha+\beta\widehat y_i+\varepsilon_i.
\]

The reference slope is one. With a meaningful positive association,
a slope greater than one can indicate insufficient dispersion of
predicted values, and a slope below one can indicate excessive
dispersion. A slope near one alone does not demonstrate calibration
of location or small errors. R04A stores an undefined slope when predictions are constant;
R04B also requires variation in the observed values. The stored
values are retained without recalculating calibration.

The following table summarizes the stored bias and slope across
each trait and model. Only finite values enter the means and sample
standard deviations; the counts show the number of contributing
splits. The slope means are model-specific available-split summaries,
not common-split contrasts. The four primary metrics and the
original comparison objects in Section 4 remain unchanged.

```{r complementary-calibration-summary}
calibration_summary <- data.frame()

for (trait in traits) {
  for (model_name in model_order) {
    if (model_name %in% gblup_models) {
      calibration_data <- gblup_results[
        gblup_results$Trait == trait & gblup_results$Model == model_name,
        , drop = FALSE
      ]
    } else {
      calibration_data <- ann_results[
        ann_results$Trait == trait & ann_results$Model == model_name,
        , drop = FALSE
      ]
    }

    bias_values <- calibration_data$Bias[is.finite(calibration_data$Bias)]
    slope_values <- calibration_data$Slope[is.finite(calibration_data$Slope)]

    calibration_summary <- rbind(calibration_summary, data.frame(
      Trait = trait,
      Model = model_name,
      Splits = nrow(calibration_data),
      Bias_N = length(bias_values),
      Bias = mean(bias_values),
      Bias_SD = sd(bias_values),
      Slope_N = length(slope_values),
      Slope = mean(slope_values),
      Slope_SD = sd(slope_values),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    ))
  }
}

knitr::kable(
  calibration_summary, format = "html", digits = 4, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Complementary bias and calibration slope on available outer splits",
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "100%")
```

### 3.3 Aggregation and individual ranking

The split-level metrics are calculated before aggregation.
For metric \(M\), let \(\mathcal{S}_M\) denote the contributing
outer splits. With finite values in those splits, the mean is

\[
\overline M=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}_M|}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{S}_M}M_k.
\]

The mean split correlation is not a correlation calculated after
pooling all held-out predictions, and mean split RMSE is generally
different from pooled RMSE. Standard deviations describe variability
across dependent splits; they are not standard errors or confidence
intervals. No \(R^2\) metric is used.

For the individual ranking, the stored OOF predictions are averaged
over the five repetitions. Global Spearman correlation, absolute
rank error and recovery of the 39 highest observed BLUPs evaluate
different aspects of individual ordering. Descending ordering does
not necessarily correspond to the biologically favorable direction
for every trait.

Pairwise linearly weighted Cohen's kappa compares the ordered
GEBV-ranking strata between two prediction models, rather than
comparing predictions with BLUP targets. The intended quintile size
is 39 individuals. The construction of the groups and the
agreement measures are addressed in Section 6.

## 4. BLUP-GEBV performance across outer splits

The object `all_results` concatenates the 225 GBLUP and 300 ANN
assessments after the metric names have been harmonized. Each row
describes a model evaluated for one trait in one outer assessment
split. No individual predictions are pooled across splits.

Three distinct comparisons are made throughout Sections 4 and 5.

| Comparison | Contributing splits | Scientific question |
|:-----------|:--------------------|:--------------------|
| Available-split summary | Finite metric values for each model separately | How does a model perform when its metric is defined? |
| Seven-model common-split correlation | The same splits with finite correlation for all seven models | How do the seven models compare on an identical subset? |
| Matched ANN-versus-GBLUP contrast | Splits with finite values for both members of a pair | What is the mean within-split difference between these two models? |

These summaries answer different questions and may give different
model orderings. The common-split comparison is conditional on the
availability of all seven correlations; it does not replace the
available-split summaries or quantify performance on excluded splits.
RMSE and MAE are finite for all 25 splits of every model and trait
in the stored analysis.

### 4.1 Combined result object

```{r combined-results}
analysis_columns <- c(
  "Dataset",
  "Trait",
  "Repetition",
  "Fold",
  "SplitID",
  "Model",
  "Pearson",
  "Spearman",
  "RMSE",
  "MAE",
  "Bias",
  "Slope"
)

all_results <- rbind(gblup_results[, analysis_columns], ann_results[, analysis_columns])

rownames(all_results) <- NULL

```

The object `model_split_structure` counts the three traits, 25 outer splits per trait, and 75 assessments for each of the seven genomic models.

```{r evaluate-model-coverage}
model_split_structure <- data.frame(
  Model = character(0),
  Traits = integer(0),
  Outer_splits_per_trait = integer(0),
  Model_trait_split_results = integer(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (model_name in model_order) {

  x <- all_results[all_results$Model == model_name,, drop = FALSE]

  split_counts <- table(x$Trait)

  model_split_structure <- rbind(
    model_split_structure,
    data.frame(
      Model = model_name,
      Traits = length(unique(x$Trait)),
      Outer_splits_per_trait = min(split_counts),
      Model_trait_split_results = nrow(x),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  )
}

model_split_structure$Model <- factor(
  model_split_structure$Model,
  levels = model_order,
  labels = model_labels
)

model_split_structure |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    caption = "Common outer-split evaluation structure by model",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
  )
```

### 4.2 Mean performance by trait and model

For each of the 21 trait-by-model combinations, the next block summarizes
only finite metric values. The mean, sample standard deviation and
number of finite values are retained separately for each metric. The
standard deviation describes variation across the outer assessment
splits, not the standard error of an independent sample.

```{r performance-summary}
# Record the mean, standard deviation, and finite-fold count for each metric.
performance_summary <- data.frame(
  Model = character(0),
  Trait = character(0),
  Splits = integer(0),
  Pearson_N = integer(0),
  Pearson = numeric(0),
  Pearson_SD = numeric(0),
  Spearman_N = integer(0),
  Spearman = numeric(0),
  Spearman_SD = numeric(0),
  RMSE_N = integer(0),
  RMSE = numeric(0),
  RMSE_SD = numeric(0),
  MAE_N = integer(0),
  MAE = numeric(0),
  MAE_SD = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (model_name in model_order) {

  for (trait in traits) {

    x <- all_results[all_results$Model == model_name & all_results$Trait == trait,, drop = FALSE]

    performance_summary <- rbind(
      performance_summary,
      data.frame(
        Model = model_name,
        Trait = trait,
        Splits = nrow(x),
        Pearson_N = sum(is.finite(x$Pearson)),
        Pearson = mean(x$Pearson[is.finite(x$Pearson)]),
        Pearson_SD = sd(x$Pearson[is.finite(x$Pearson)]),
        Spearman_N = sum(is.finite(x$Spearman)),
        Spearman = mean(x$Spearman[is.finite(x$Spearman)]),
        Spearman_SD = sd(x$Spearman[is.finite(x$Spearman)]),
        RMSE_N = sum(is.finite(x$RMSE)),
        RMSE = mean(x$RMSE[is.finite(x$RMSE)]),
        RMSE_SD = sd(x$RMSE[is.finite(x$RMSE)]),
        MAE_N = sum(is.finite(x$MAE)),
        MAE = mean(x$MAE[is.finite(x$MAE)]),
        MAE_SD = sd(x$MAE[is.finite(x$MAE)]),
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      )
    )
  }
}

```

The object `performance_summary` retains the original column structure
and all four primary metrics. It is sorted by trait and scientific
model order before presentation. The association and error summaries

For Cer and BM, both correlations are available in all 25 splits for
every model. For LP, GBLUP_A has 23 finite values, GBLUP_AD and
GBLUP_ADE each have 24, and each ANN has 25. Thus 521 of the 525
stored assessments contribute to each correlation summary. The four
constant-prediction assessments in LP remain valid for the error
metrics. The bias and slope summaries are presented in Section 3.2.

For Cer and BM, GBLUP_A has the highest mean Pearson and Spearman
among the seven methods. For LP, the available-split means use
different sets of assessments and are not directly comparable as
matched estimates.

### 4.3 Common finite splits for direct correlation comparison

When a model produces a constant prediction in an outer split, Pearson and
Spearman are undefined for that split. The descriptive model summaries above
retain every finite value available for each model. A direct cross-model
comparison, however, should use the same outer splits for all seven models.

For each trait, the expected split identifiers are obtained from
the R03 result keys constructed in Section 2.5. A split is eligible
only when its repetition and fold match the design and it has exactly
one record from each of the seven models. Pearson and Spearman
availability are evaluated separately.

For correlation metric \(M\), let \(S_{t,m,M}\) be the set of
eligible splits with a finite value for trait \(t\) and model \(m\).
The common subset is

\[
C_{t,M}=\bigcap_{m=1}^{7} S_{t,m,M}.
\]

The comparable mean for model \(m\) is its arithmetic mean over
\(C_{t,M}\). This excludes an entire trait-by-split comparison
when any one model lacks a finite value for the given metric.
No split is excluded from the error comparisons in the stored results.

The next block records the eligibility and availability for each
of the 75 expected trait-by-split combinations. It retains the
original `common_correlation_summary` structure for the subsequent
figures and exports.

```{r common-finite-correlation-splits}
# Record split eligibility separately from the correlation summaries.
common_split_coverage <- data.frame()
common_correlation_summary <- data.frame(
  Model = character(0),
  Trait = character(0),
  Pearson_Common_N = integer(0),
  Pearson_Common = numeric(0),
  Spearman_Common_N = integer(0),
  Spearman_Common = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (trait in traits) {

  trait_results <- all_results[all_results$Trait == trait,, drop = FALSE]

  expected_splits <- expected_result_keys[
    expected_result_keys$Trait == trait, , drop = FALSE
  ]
  split_ids <- sort(unique(expected_splits$SplitID))

  pearson_common_splits <- character(0)
  spearman_common_splits <- character(0)

  for (split_id in split_ids) {

    split_data <- trait_results[trait_results$SplitID == split_id,, drop = FALSE]

    expected_split <- expected_splits[
      expected_splits$SplitID == split_id, , drop = FALSE
    ]
    model_complete <- nrow(split_data) == length(model_order) &&
      !anyNA(split_data$Model) &&
      !anyDuplicated(split_data$Model) &&
      setequal(split_data$Model, model_order)
    design_match <- nrow(expected_split) == 1L &&
      nrow(split_data) > 0L &&
      !anyNA(split_data[, c("Repetition", "Fold")]) &&
      all(split_data$Repetition == expected_split$Repetition) &&
      all(split_data$Fold == expected_split$Fold)

    pearson_common <- model_complete && design_match &&
      all(is.finite(split_data$Pearson))
    spearman_common <- model_complete && design_match &&
      all(is.finite(split_data$Spearman))

    common_split_coverage <- rbind(
      common_split_coverage,
      data.frame(
        Trait = trait, SplitID = split_id,
        Records = nrow(split_data),
        Distinct_models = length(unique(split_data$Model)),
        Complete_models = model_complete,
        Design_match = design_match,
        Pearson_finite = sum(is.finite(split_data$Pearson)),
        Spearman_finite = sum(is.finite(split_data$Spearman)),
        Pearson_common = pearson_common,
        Spearman_common = spearman_common,
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      )
    )

    if (pearson_common) {
      pearson_common_splits <- c(pearson_common_splits, split_id)
    }

    if (spearman_common) {
      spearman_common_splits <- c(spearman_common_splits, split_id)
    }
  }

  for (model_name in model_order) {

    pearson_values <- trait_results$Pearson[
      trait_results$Model == model_name & trait_results$SplitID %in% pearson_common_splits
    ]

    spearman_values <- trait_results$Spearman[
      trait_results$Model == model_name & trait_results$SplitID %in% spearman_common_splits
    ]

    common_correlation_summary <- rbind(
      common_correlation_summary,
      data.frame(
        Model = model_name,
        Trait = trait,
        Pearson_Common_N = length(pearson_common_splits),
        Pearson_Common = mean(pearson_values),
        Spearman_Common_N = length(spearman_common_splits),
        Spearman_Common = mean(spearman_values),
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      )
    )
  }
}

```

The eligibility summary counts complete model sets, design matches
and common finite splits. The excluded-split table identifies any
split not retained for at least one correlation.

```{r display-common-split-coverage}
common_split_counts <- aggregate(
  cbind(Complete_models, Design_match, Pearson_common, Spearman_common) ~ Trait,
  data = common_split_coverage,
  FUN = sum
)
common_split_counts <- common_split_counts[
  match(traits, common_split_counts$Trait), , drop = FALSE
]
rownames(common_split_counts) <- NULL

knitr::kable(
  common_split_counts, format = "html", row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Eligible and common finite outer splits by trait",
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
)
```

```{r display-excluded-correlation-splits}

  !common_split_coverage$Pearson_common |
    !common_split_coverage$Spearman_common, , drop = FALSE
]

knitr::kable(
  excluded_correlation_splits, format = "html", row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Outer splits excluded from at least one seven-model correlation comparison",
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "100%")
```

For each trait, `common_correlation_summary` reports the mean
correlations using the eligible common sets. Counts are reported
separately for each metric.

  labels = model_labels
)

common_correlation_display |>

```

For Cer and BM, all 25 splits contribute to both common sets.
For LP, 23 splits contribute to each. On those common splits,
GBLUP_A, GBLUP_AD and GBLUP_ADE have mean Pearson correlations
of approximately 0.2073, 0.1990 and 0.1975, respectively, while
ANN_L2 has 0.1762. In contrast, the available-split means of
ANN_L2 (0.1918), GBLUP_AD (0.1742) and GBLUP_ADE (0.1728)
give a different ordering. The common subset makes the compared
means refer to identical assessments, but does not eliminate the
scientific relevance of undefined correlations.

### 4.4 Best predictive metrics by trait

The next table identifies the highest common-split mean correlation
and lowest mean BLUP-GEBV error separately. All models with exactly
the same optimal finite value at full stored precision are retained.
If several models share an optimum, their identifiers are joined
in the existing character column in model order. Equality after
rounding alone is not a numerical tie; neither a unique optimum
nor a tie establishes statistical superiority.

```{r predictive-winners}
predictive_winners <- data.frame(
  Trait = character(0),
  Pearson_Common_N = integer(0),
  Best_Pearson_Model = character(0),
  Best_Pearson = numeric(0),
  Spearman_Common_N = integer(0),
  Best_Spearman_Model = character(0),
  Best_Spearman = numeric(0),
  Best_RMSE_Model = character(0),
  Best_RMSE = numeric(0),
  Best_MAE_Model = character(0),
  Best_MAE = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (trait in traits) {

  x <- performance_summary[performance_summary$Trait == trait,, drop = FALSE]

  correlation_x <- common_correlation_summary[common_correlation_summary$Trait == trait,, drop = FALSE]

  pearson_best <- if (any(is.finite(correlation_x$Pearson_Common))) {
    max(correlation_x$Pearson_Common[is.finite(correlation_x$Pearson_Common)])
  } else NA_real_
  pearson_index <- which(is.finite(correlation_x$Pearson_Common) &
    correlation_x$Pearson_Common == pearson_best)

  spearman_best <- if (any(is.finite(correlation_x$Spearman_Common))) {
    max(correlation_x$Spearman_Common[is.finite(correlation_x$Spearman_Common)])
  } else NA_real_
  spearman_index <- which(is.finite(correlation_x$Spearman_Common) &
    correlation_x$Spearman_Common == spearman_best)

  rmse_best <- if (any(is.finite(x$RMSE))) {
    min(x$RMSE[is.finite(x$RMSE)])
  } else NA_real_
  rmse_index <- which(is.finite(x$RMSE) &
    x$RMSE == rmse_best)

  mae_best <- if (any(is.finite(x$MAE))) {
    min(x$MAE[is.finite(x$MAE)])
  } else NA_real_
  mae_index <- which(is.finite(x$MAE) &
    x$MAE == mae_best)

  predictive_winners <- rbind(
    predictive_winners,
    data.frame(
      Trait = trait,
      Pearson_Common_N = unique(correlation_x$Pearson_Common_N),
      Best_Pearson_Model = if (length(pearson_index)) {
        paste(model_order[model_order %in% correlation_x$Model[pearson_index]], collapse = ", ")
      } else NA_character_,
      Best_Pearson = pearson_best,
      Spearman_Common_N = unique(correlation_x$Spearman_Common_N),
      Best_Spearman_Model = if (length(spearman_index)) {
        paste(model_order[model_order %in% correlation_x$Model[spearman_index]], collapse = ", ")
      } else NA_character_,
      Best_Spearman = spearman_best,
      Best_RMSE_Model = if (length(rmse_index)) {
        paste(model_order[model_order %in% x$Model[rmse_index]], collapse = ", ")
      } else NA_character_,
      Best_RMSE = rmse_best,
      Best_MAE_Model = if (length(mae_index)) {
        paste(model_order[model_order %in% x$Model[mae_index]], collapse = ", ")
      } else NA_character_,
      Best_MAE = mae_best,
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  )
}

```

The object `predictive_winners` identifies the models with the highest common-split Pearson and Spearman correlations and the lowest RMSE and MAE for each trait.

```{r display-predictive-winners}
PREDICTIVE_WINNERS_CSV <- file.path(COMPARISON_DIR, "real_model_predictive_winners.csv")

predictive_winners |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Best predictive metric by trait; correlations use common finite outer splits across all seven models",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
  ) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "100%")
```

```{r save-predictive-winners, eval=FALSE}
write.csv(predictive_winners, PREDICTIVE_WINNERS_CSV, row.names = FALSE)
```

For the archived results, GBLUP_A has the highest mean correlations
on common splits and the smallest mean RMSE for all three traits.
It also has the smallest mean MAE for Cer and LP; GBLUP_AD has
the smallest mean MAE for BM. These are descriptive extrema, not
a single universal ranking across criteria.

### 4.5 Distribution of split-level performance

The boxplots show available split-level values. Boxes span the first
and third quartiles, central lines represent medians, whiskers
extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 interquartile ranges,
and white diamonds represent arithmetic means. Individual points
show split-level metric values rather than individual BLUPs.
Both correlation boxplots use the fixed theoretical range from -1 to 1;
only finite values enter their distributions. The named GDocs palette follows
the seven-model order of M05 and is reused in all categorical plots here.
The Spearman heatmap instead displays common-split mean correlations
from Section 4.3. Its cells therefore need not equal the available-split
means when some correlations are undefined. RMSE and MAE use
trait-specific scales and should be compared within each trait.

```{r prepare-performance-plots}
plot_results <- all_results

plot_results$Model <- factor(plot_results$Model, levels = model_order, labels = model_labels)

plot_results$Trait <- factor(plot_results$Trait, levels = traits)

# Use the same named palette for every categorical model display.
model_colors <- setNames(ggthemes::gdocs_pal()(length(model_labels)), model_labels)
```

```{r pearson-comparison, fig.width=12, fig.height=5.8, fig.cap="Pearson correlations on available outer splits. Each point represents a finite split value; white diamonds indicate model means.", fig.alt="Boxplots of Pearson with individual split values and mean diamonds for seven models in three traits."}
p_pearson <- ggplot(
  plot_results[is.finite(plot_results$Pearson), , drop = FALSE],
  aes(x = Model, y = Pearson, fill = Model)
) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, color = "grey50") + geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.58,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    alpha = 0.70,
    na.rm = TRUE
  ) + geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.10, height = 0, seed = 20261105L + 701L),
    alpha = 0.30,
    size = 1.2,
    na.rm = TRUE
  ) + stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "point",
    shape = 23,
    size = 3.0,
    fill = "white",
    na.rm = TRUE
  ) + facet_wrap(
    ~ Trait,
    nrow = 1,
    scales = "fixed"
  ) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-1, 1), breaks = seq(-1, 1, by = 0.5)) + scale_fill_manual(values = model_colors) + labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Pearson correlation",
    fill = NULL
  ) + theme_gdocs() + theme(legend.position = "none", axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1))

print(p_pearson)
```

```{r save-pearson-comparison-tiff, eval=TRUE, include=FALSE}
ggsave(
  file.path(FIGURE_DIR, "real_comparison_pearson_by_model_trait.tiff"),
  plot = p_pearson,
  device = "tiff",
  width = 12,
  height = 5.8,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 300,
  compression = "lzw"
)
```

The same representation is used for Spearman on available outer splits.
It complements, rather than replaces, the common-split heatmap below.

Each point represents a finite split value; white diamonds indicate model means.", fig.alt="Boxplots of Spearman with individual split values and mean diamonds for seven models in three traits."}

```{r spearman-comparison, fig.width=10.5, fig.height=5.8, fig.cap="Spearman correlation between BLUP and GEBV for the seven genomic models. For each trait, the heatmap uses the outer splits in which Spearman is finite for all seven models.", fig.alt="Annotated seven-model by three-trait Spearman heatmap with a fixed correlation scale from minus one to one."}

    scales = "free_y"
  ) + scale_fill_manual(values = model_colors) + labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "MAE",
    fill = NULL
  ) + theme_gdocs() + theme(legend.position = "none", axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1))

print(p_mae)
```

  file.path(FIGURE_DIR, "real_comparison_mae_by_model_trait.tiff"),
  plot = p_mae,
  device = "tiff",
  width = 12,
  height = 5.8,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 300,
  compression = "lzw"

```

## 5. Matched ANN-versus-GBLUP outer-split contrasts

### 5.1 Definition of the matched contrasts

The common assessment keys validated in Section 2 permit comparisons
of every ANN variant with every GBLUP structure within the same trait
and outer split. There are 12 model pairs per trait and 36
trait-by-pair combinations.

For a fixed trait and model pair, let \(k\) denote the matched split,
\(A\) denote the ANN variant and \(G\) denote the GBLUP structure.
For either correlation \(r\) (Pearson or Spearman), define

\[
d_{r,k}=r_{A,k}-r_{G,k}.
\]

For the error metrics, reverse the direction:

\[
d_{\mathrm{RMSE},k}=\mathrm{RMSE}_{G,k}-\mathrm{RMSE}_{A,k},
\qquad
d_{\mathrm{MAE},k}=\mathrm{MAE}_{G,k}-\mathrm{MAE}_{A,k}.
\]

For each metric \(M\), let \(P_M\) be the set of matched splits
where both models have finite values. The mean contrast is

\[
\overline d_M=\frac{1}{|P_M|}\sum_{k\in P_M}d_{M,k}.
\]

A positive value favors ANN, a negative value favors GBLUP, and
zero indicates equal mean performance for that pair and metric
on its contributing splits. These differences are on the original
metric scale, not percentages. Pair-specific finite sets can be
larger than the seven-model common set in Section 4.3.

### 5.2 Calculation and presentation

The original matched calculation is retained. Each pair is joined
on repetition, fold and split identifier within a fixed trait.
Finite-value filtering is applied separately to each metric.

```{r matched-family-contrasts}
split_keys <- c("Repetition", "Fold", "SplitID")

# Calculate matched ANN-minus-GBLUP advantages for all model-family pairs.
paired_summary <- data.frame(
  Trait = character(0),
  GBLUP = character(0),
  ANN = character(0),
  Pearson_N = integer(0),
  Mean_Pearson_Advantage = numeric(0),
  Spearman_N = integer(0),
  Mean_Spearman_Advantage = numeric(0),
  RMSE_N = integer(0),
  Mean_RMSE_Advantage = numeric(0),
  MAE_N = integer(0),
  Mean_MAE_Advantage = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (trait in traits) {

  for (gblup_model in gblup_models) {

    for (ann_model in ann_models) {

      g <- all_results[
        all_results$Trait == trait & all_results$Model == gblup_model,
        c(split_keys, "Pearson", "Spearman", "RMSE", "MAE"),
        drop = FALSE
      ]

      a <- all_results[
        all_results$Trait == trait & all_results$Model == ann_model,
        c(split_keys, "Pearson", "Spearman", "RMSE", "MAE"),
        drop = FALSE
      ]

      matched <- merge(a, g, by = split_keys, suffixes = c("_ANN", "_GBLUP"), all = FALSE, sort = FALSE)

      pearson_finite <- is.finite(matched$Pearson_ANN) & is.finite(matched$Pearson_GBLUP)

      spearman_finite <- is.finite(matched$Spearman_ANN) & is.finite(matched$Spearman_GBLUP)

      rmse_finite <- is.finite(matched$RMSE_ANN) & is.finite(matched$RMSE_GBLUP)

      mae_finite <- is.finite(matched$MAE_ANN) & is.finite(matched$MAE_GBLUP)

      paired_summary <- rbind(
        paired_summary,
        data.frame(
          Trait = trait,
          GBLUP = gblup_model,
          ANN = ann_model,
          Pearson_N = sum(pearson_finite),
          Mean_Pearson_Advantage = mean(
              matched$Pearson_ANN[
                pearson_finite
              ] - matched$Pearson_GBLUP[pearson_finite]
            ),
          Spearman_N = sum(spearman_finite),
          Mean_Spearman_Advantage = mean(
              matched$Spearman_ANN[
                spearman_finite
              ] - matched$Spearman_GBLUP[spearman_finite]
            ),
          RMSE_N = sum(rmse_finite),
          Mean_RMSE_Advantage = mean(matched$RMSE_GBLUP[rmse_finite] - matched$RMSE_ANN[rmse_finite]),
          MAE_N = sum(mae_finite),
          Mean_MAE_Advantage = mean(matched$MAE_GBLUP[mae_finite] - matched$MAE_ANN[mae_finite]),
          stringsAsFactors = FALSE
        )
      )
    }
  }
}

```

The object `paired_summary` contains 36 contrasts: three traits, three GBLUP structures, and four ANN variants. Each contrast is calculated within matched outer splits; positive advantages favour ANN under the metric-specific sign convention stated above.

```{r display-matched-contrasts}
PAIRED_SUMMARY_CSV <- file.path(COMPARISON_DIR, "real_ann_vs_gblup_matched_summary.csv")

paired_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Matched ANN-versus-GBLUP mean performance advantage; positive values favor ANN",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
  ) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "100%")
```

```{r save-matched-contrasts, eval=FALSE}
write.csv(paired_summary, PAIRED_SUMMARY_CSV, row.names = FALSE)
```

### 5.3 Interpretation of the matched contrasts

The next table describes the range of mean contrasts over the 12
model pairs for each trait and metric. The positive, zero and
negative counts refer to model pairs, not individual outer splits
or independent experiments. The original pair-specific results
remain in the preceding table.

```{r matched-contrast-interpretation}
contrast_ranges <- data.frame()

for (trait in traits) {
  trait_pairs <- paired_summary[paired_summary$Trait == trait, , drop = FALSE]
  for (metric in c("Pearson", "Spearman", "RMSE", "MAE")) {
    values <- trait_pairs[[paste0("Mean_", metric, "_Advantage")]]
    finite_values <- values[is.finite(values)]
    contrast_ranges <- rbind(
      contrast_ranges,
      data.frame(
        Trait = trait,
        Metric = metric,
        Pairs = length(values),
        Finite_pairs = length(finite_values),
        Minimum = if (length(finite_values)) min(finite_values) else NA_real_,
        Maximum = if (length(finite_values)) max(finite_values) else NA_real_,
        Favors_ANN = sum(finite_values > 0),
        Equal_mean = sum(finite_values == 0),
        Favors_GBLUP = sum(finite_values < 0),
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      )
    )
  }
}

knitr::kable(
  contrast_ranges, format = "html", digits = 4, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Range and direction of matched mean contrasts across model pairs",
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "100%")
```

The following dot plot preserves each of the 12 individual model pairs.
Each panel has its own horizontal range, because RMSE and MAE are
trait-specific and the four metrics are not on a common scale.
The vertical zero line separates advantages for GBLUP and ANN.
Points are mean matched differences, not confidence intervals.

```{r matched-contrast-figure, fig.width=15, fig.height=12, fig.cap="Mean matched contrasts for the twelve ANN-versus-GBLUP pairs in each trait and metric. Positive differences favor ANN; horizontal scales are panel-specific.", fig.alt="Twelve dot plot panels of matched mean contrasts, showing each model pair and a zero reference line."}
contrast_plot_data <- data.frame()
contrast_pair_levels <- character(0)

for (gblup_model in gblup_models) {
  for (ann_model in ann_models) {
    contrast_pair_levels <- c(contrast_pair_levels, paste(
      model_labels[match(ann_model, model_order)],
      model_labels[match(gblup_model, model_order)], sep = " / "
    ))
  }
}

for (metric in c("Pearson", "Spearman", "RMSE", "MAE")) {
  contrast_plot_data <- rbind(contrast_plot_data, data.frame(
    Trait = paired_summary$Trait,
    Pair = paste(
      model_labels[match(paired_summary$ANN, model_order)],
      model_labels[match(paired_summary$GBLUP, model_order)], sep = " / "
    ),
    ANN = model_labels[match(paired_summary$ANN, model_order)],
    Metric = metric,
    Difference = paired_summary[[paste0("Mean_", metric, "_Advantage")]],
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ))
}

contrast_plot_data$Trait <- factor(contrast_plot_data$Trait, levels = traits)
contrast_plot_data$Metric <- factor(
  contrast_plot_data$Metric, levels = c("Pearson", "Spearman", "RMSE", "MAE")
)
contrast_plot_data$Pair <- factor(contrast_plot_data$Pair, levels = rev(contrast_pair_levels))
contrast_plot_data$ANN <- factor(
  contrast_plot_data$ANN, levels = model_labels[match(ann_models, model_order)]
)

p_matched_contrasts <- ggplot(
  contrast_plot_data, aes(x = Difference, y = Pair, color = ANN)
) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, color = "grey50") +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  facet_wrap(vars(Trait, Metric), ncol = 4, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_color_manual(values = model_colors) +
  labs(x = "Mean matched difference", y = NULL, color = "ANN variant") +
  theme_gdocs() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

print(p_matched_contrasts)
```

```{r save-matched-contrast-figure-tiff, eval=TRUE, include=FALSE}
ggsave(
  file.path(FIGURE_DIR, "real_comparison_matched_contrasts.tiff"),
  plot = p_matched_contrasts, device = "tiff", width = 15, height = 12,
  units = "in", dpi = 300, compression = "lzw"
)
```

For Cer and BM, all 12 pairs favor GBLUP in the mean contrast
for each of the four primary metrics. For LP, some pairwise
correlation contrasts favor ANN, although all RMSE and MAE
contrasts favor GBLUP. The positive LP correlation contrasts
are compatible with the seven-model common-split results: the
matched pairwise summaries may use 23 or 24 finite splits,
whereas the seven-model comparison uses 23. RMSE and MAE
contrasts use all 25 splits for every pair.

A positive mean contrast does not imply that ANN outperforms GBLUP
in every split. Similarly, a negative mean contrast does not
establish statistical superiority. The repeated outer splits share
analysis individuals, and the pairwise comparisons reuse the same
models and assessment data. No significance tests or independent
replicate confidence intervals are inferred from these summaries.
The individual ranking results in Section 6 address a different
evaluation criterion.


## 6. Global ranking

The ranking analysis compares individuals rather than individual
outer assessment splits. For each trait and model, the five held-out
predictions for individual \(i\) are averaged before ranking:

\[
\overline{\widehat y}_i=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{r=1}^{5}\widehat y_{ir},
\qquad
s_i=\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}\sum_{r=1}^{5}
(\widehat y_{ir}-\overline{\widehat y}_i)^2}.
\]

The mean and sample standard deviation are stored in the R04A
and R04B ranking files. The standard deviation describes variation
among repeated OOF predictions, not a prediction interval or standard
error. The ranks are calculated from the mean predictions, not
from averages of fold-specific ranks.

The 20,475 held-out predictions correspond to 4,095 individual
records: 195 individuals for each of the 21 trait-by-model
combinations. This section retains the stored individual means,
standard deviations, ranks and selection indicators.

### 6.1 Combined individual ranking object

Before selecting the shared columns, examine the stored `N_OOF`
values and the individual identifiers against the R03 population.
The expected result is 195 distinct individuals, five predictions
per individual, and 39 observed and predicted upper-group members
in every combination.

```{r ranking-oof-coverage}
ranking_coverage <- data.frame()
ranking_expected_ids <- as.character(comparison_cv$ids)

for (trait in traits) {
  for (model_name in model_order) {
    if (model_name %in% gblup_models) {
      ranking_input <- gblup_ranking[
        gblup_ranking$Trait == trait & gblup_ranking$Model == model_name,
        , drop = FALSE
      ]
    } else {
      ranking_input <- ann_ranking[
        ann_ranking$Trait == trait & ann_ranking$Model == model_name,
        , drop = FALSE
      ]
    }
    ranking_coverage <- rbind(ranking_coverage, data.frame(
      Trait = trait, Model = model_name,
      Individuals = nrow(ranking_input),
      Distinct_IDs = length(unique(ranking_input$ID)),
      Missing_IDs = length(setdiff(ranking_expected_ids, ranking_input$ID)),
      Unexpected_IDs = length(setdiff(ranking_input$ID, ranking_expected_ids)),
      OOF_Min = min(ranking_input$N_OOF),
      OOF_Max = max(ranking_input$N_OOF),
      OOF_not_five = sum(is.na(ranking_input$N_OOF) | ranking_input$N_OOF != 5L),
      Observed_Top20_N = sum(ranking_input$BLUP_Top20),
      Predicted_Top20_N = sum(ranking_input$GEBV_Top20),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    ))
  }
}

knitr::kable(
  ranking_coverage, format = "html", row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Individual ranking coverage and stored OOF prediction counts",
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "100%")
```

The shared object combines the original ranking columns without
altering their values or the underlying RDS files.

```{r combined-ranking}
ranking_columns <- c(
  "Model",
  "Trait",
  "ID",
  "BLUP",
  "GEBV",
  "GEBV_SD",
  "BLUP_Rank",
  "GEBV_Rank",
  "Rank_Difference",
  "Absolute_Rank_Error",
  "BLUP_Top20",
  "GEBV_Top20"
)

all_ranking <- rbind(gblup_ranking[, ranking_columns], ann_ranking[, ranking_columns])

rownames(all_ranking) <- NULL

```

The objects `gblup_ranking` and `ann_ranking` contain the GEBVs calculated
from five held-out predictions per individual, trait, and model in R04A and
R04B. The object `all_ranking` combines those individual records without
recalculating their means.

### 6.2 Ranking summary

Within each trait-model combination, the observed BLUP and mean
predicted BLUP are ranked in decreasing order. Rank 1 is the
largest value, and tied values receive their average rank.
Let \(R_i\) and \(\widehat R_i\) be the observed and predicted
ranks, respectively. Define

\[
D_i=\widehat R_i-R_i,\qquad E_i=|D_i|.
\]

A positive difference places the individual farther down the predicted
ranking. The mean and median absolute rank errors describe displacement
across the 195 individuals. Global Spearman is

\[
\rho_{\mathrm{global}}=\operatorname{cor}_{S}
(R_i,\widehat R_i),\qquad
\operatorname{MARE}=\frac{1}{195}\sum_{i=1}^{195}E_i.
\]

This is a correlation across the population's individual OOF
rankings, not the mean of the split-level correlations.

The upper-group size is \(n_s=\lceil0.20\times195\rceil=39\).
Let \(S_o\) and \(S_p\) be the sets of the 39 highest observed and
mean predicted BLUPs, respectively. The stored selection indicators
use decreasing values with individual ID as the deterministic
secondary ordering criterion. This rule does not change average
ranks used in rank errors and correlation.

\[
N_{\mathrm{overlap}}=|S_o\cap S_p|,
\qquad
p_{\mathrm{overlap}}=\frac{|S_o\cap S_p|}{39}.
\]

The overlap rate is a recovery fraction, not a correlation,
chance-corrected index or estimate of genetic gain. The descending
order is retained for all three traits; the upper group is not
necessarily the biologically desirable group for every breeding
objective.

The following block summarizes the original individual ranks and
selection indicators without redefining them.

```{r ranking-summary}
# Compare the 195-individual rankings after aggregating five held-out predictions.
ranking_summary <- data.frame(
  Model = character(0),
  Trait = character(0),
  Individuals = integer(0),
  Ranking_Spearman = numeric(0),
  Mean_Absolute_Rank_Error = numeric(0),
  Median_Absolute_Rank_Error = numeric(0),
  Top20_N = integer(0),
  Top20_Overlap_N = integer(0),
  Top20_Overlap_Rate = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (model_name in model_order) {

  for (trait in traits) {

    x <- all_ranking[all_ranking$Model == model_name & all_ranking$Trait == trait,, drop = FALSE]

    overlap_n <- sum(x$BLUP_Top20 & x$GEBV_Top20)

    ranking_summary <- rbind(
      ranking_summary,
      data.frame(
        Model = model_name,
        Trait = trait,
        Individuals = nrow(x),
        Ranking_Spearman = cor(x$BLUP_Rank, x$GEBV_Rank, method = "spearman"),
        Mean_Absolute_Rank_Error = mean(x$Absolute_Rank_Error),
        Median_Absolute_Rank_Error = median(x$Absolute_Rank_Error),
        Top20_N = 39L,
        Top20_Overlap_N = overlap_n,
        Top20_Overlap_Rate = overlap_n / 39L,
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      )
    )
  }
}

```

The object `ranking_summary` compares global BLUP–GEBV rank correlation, absolute rank error, and the number of BLUP top-20% individuals recovered by GEBV rankings among all 195 individuals.

```{r display-ranking-summary}
ranking_summary$Trait <- factor(ranking_summary$Trait, levels = traits)

ranking_summary$Model <- factor(ranking_summary$Model, levels = model_order)

ranking_summary <- ranking_summary[order(ranking_summary$Trait, ranking_summary$Model),, drop = FALSE]

ranking_summary$Trait <- as.character(ranking_summary$Trait)

ranking_summary$Model <- as.character(ranking_summary$Model)

RANKING_SUMMARY_CSV <- file.path(COMPARISON_DIR, "real_model_ranking_summary.csv")

ranking_display <- ranking_summary
ranking_display$Model <- factor(ranking_display$Model, levels = model_order, labels = model_labels)

ranking_display |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Global BLUP-GEBV ranking and top-20% selection",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
  ) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "100%")
```

```{r save-ranking-summary, eval=FALSE}
write.csv(ranking_summary, RANKING_SUMMARY_CSV, row.names = FALSE)
```

Split-level Spearman and global ranking Spearman answer different questions.
Split-level Spearman evaluates BLUP-GEBV ranking agreement among the 39
assessment individuals in one outer split. Global ranking Spearman evaluates
BLUP-GEBV ranking agreement among all 195 individuals after the GEBV of each
individual is obtained from its five predictions.

### 6.3 Ranking winners by trait

The three criteria are considered separately. All models with the
same optimal finite value at full precision are retained in model
order. For top-20% recovery, the integer overlap count determines
the optimum because the denominator is fixed at 39. A tied optimum
does not imply that the selected sets of individuals are identical,
nor does a unique optimum establish statistical superiority.

```{r ranking-winners}
ranking_winners <- data.frame(
  Trait = character(0),
  Best_Ranking_Spearman_Model = character(0),
  Best_Ranking_Spearman = numeric(0),
  Best_Mean_Rank_Error_Model = character(0),
  Best_Mean_Rank_Error = numeric(0),
  Best_Top20_Model = character(0),
  Best_Top20_Overlap_N = integer(0),
  Best_Top20_Overlap_Rate = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (trait in traits) {

  x <- ranking_summary[ranking_summary$Trait == trait,, drop = FALSE]

  ranking_best <- if (any(is.finite(x$Ranking_Spearman))) {
    max(x$Ranking_Spearman[is.finite(x$Ranking_Spearman)])
  } else NA_real_
  ranking_index <- which(is.finite(x$Ranking_Spearman) & x$Ranking_Spearman == ranking_best)

  rank_error_best <- if (any(is.finite(x$Mean_Absolute_Rank_Error))) {
    min(x$Mean_Absolute_Rank_Error[is.finite(x$Mean_Absolute_Rank_Error)])
  } else NA_real_
  rank_error_index <- which(is.finite(x$Mean_Absolute_Rank_Error) & x$Mean_Absolute_Rank_Error == rank_error_best)

  top20_best <- if (any(is.finite(x$Top20_Overlap_N))) {
    max(x$Top20_Overlap_N[is.finite(x$Top20_Overlap_N)])
  } else NA_integer_
  top20_index <- which(is.finite(x$Top20_Overlap_N) & x$Top20_Overlap_N == top20_best)

  ranking_winners <- rbind(
    ranking_winners,
    data.frame(
      Trait = trait,
      Best_Ranking_Spearman_Model = if (length(ranking_index)) {
        paste(model_order[model_order %in% x$Model[ranking_index]], collapse = ", ")
      } else NA_character_,
      Best_Ranking_Spearman = ranking_best,
      Best_Mean_Rank_Error_Model = if (length(rank_error_index)) {
        paste(model_order[model_order %in% x$Model[rank_error_index]], collapse = ", ")
      } else NA_character_,
      Best_Mean_Rank_Error = rank_error_best,
      Best_Top20_Model = if (length(top20_index)) {
        paste(model_order[model_order %in% x$Model[top20_index]], collapse = ", ")
      } else NA_character_,
      Best_Top20_Overlap_N = top20_best,
      Best_Top20_Overlap_Rate = top20_best / 39L,
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  )
}

```

The object `ranking_winners` identifies the strongest global ranking correlation, smallest mean rank error, and largest top-20% overlap for each trait. These selection criteria are kept separate.

```{r display-ranking-winners}
RANKING_WINNERS_CSV <- file.path(COMPARISON_DIR, "real_model_ranking_winners.csv")

ranking_winners |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Best global ranking and top-20% selection metric for each trait",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
  ) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "100%")
```

```{r save-ranking-winners, eval=TRUE, include=FALSE}
write.csv(ranking_winners, RANKING_WINNERS_CSV, row.names = FALSE)
```

In the stored results, GBLUP_A has the highest global Spearman
and lowest mean absolute rank error for Cer; ANN_0 has those
descriptive optima for BM, and ANN_L2 for LP. The three GBLUP
structures tie for the largest Cer upper-group recovery (22 of 39).
ANN_0 recovers 12 of 39 for BM and ANN_L1_L2 recovers 13 of 39
for LP. The ranking criteria therefore need not favor the model
with the highest mean split-level association or lowest mean
prediction error in Section 4.

### 6.4 Ranking comparison figures

The heatmap reports global Spearman for each of the seven models
and three traits. The bar chart reports the number of observed
upper-group individuals recovered by each model, out of 39.

```{r ranking-spearman-figure, fig.width=10.5, fig.height=5.8, fig.cap="Global Spearman correlation between the BLUP ranking and the GEBV ranking for the seven genomic models.", fig.alt="Annotated seven-model by three-trait Spearman heatmap with a fixed correlation scale from minus one to one."}
ranking_plot <- ranking_summary

ranking_plot$Model <- factor(ranking_plot$Model, levels = rev(model_order), labels = rev(model_labels))

ranking_plot$Trait <- factor(ranking_plot$Trait, levels = traits)

ranking_plot$Text_color <- ifelse(
  abs(ranking_plot$Ranking_Spearman) >= 0.65,
  "white",
  "black"
)

p_ranking_spearman <- ggplot(
  ranking_plot,
  aes(x = Trait, y = Model, fill = Ranking_Spearman)
) + geom_tile(
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) + geom_text(

    size = 4.2,

  ) + scale_color_identity() + scale_fill_gradient2(
    name = "Spearman",

  ) + labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) + theme_gdocs() + theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

print(p_ranking_spearman)
```

```{r top20-figure, fig.width=12, fig.height=5.8, fig.alt="Faceted bar chart of recovered individuals out of 39 for seven models and three traits.", fig.cap="BLUP top-20% individuals recovered by the GEBV ranking for each genomic model. Each top-20% set contains exactly 39 individuals."}
top20_plot <- ranking_summary

top20_plot$Model <- factor(top20_plot$Model, levels = model_order, labels = model_labels)

top20_plot$Trait <- factor(top20_plot$Trait, levels = traits)

p_top20 <- ggplot(
  top20_plot,
  aes(x = Model, y = Top20_Overlap_N, fill = Model)
) + geom_col(width = 0.72) + facet_wrap(
    ~ Trait,
    nrow = 1
  ) + scale_fill_manual(values = model_colors) + scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 39),
    breaks = c(0, 10, 20, 30, 39)
  ) + labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "BLUP top-20% individuals recovered",
    fill = NULL
  ) + theme_gdocs() + theme(legend.position = "none", axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1))

print(p_top20)
```

### 6.5 Pairwise agreement among GEBV-ranking quintiles

Spearman correlation compares the ordering of BLUPs and GEBVs within each
model. A separate question is whether different genomic models assign the same
individuals to similar **selection strata** based on their GEBV rankings.

For each trait and model, the intended five strata consist of
39 individuals each, ordered from the highest to the lowest GEBV:

- quintile 1: ranks 1--39;
- quintile 2: ranks 40--78;
- quintile 3: ranks 79--117;
- quintile 4: ranks 118--156;
- quintile 5: ranks 157--195.

Pairwise agreement among these ordered GEBV-ranking quintiles is quantified
with **linearly weighted Cohen's kappa**. All 21 unordered pairs formed by the
seven genomic methods are evaluated individually within each trait. No method
family is pooled, averaged, or otherwise aggregated for this comparison.
Identical quintile assignments receive full weight, whereas disagreement
receives progressively smaller weight as the distance between quintiles
increases. This provides a chance-corrected measure of agreement in selection
strata rather than a second measure of exact rank-position displacement.

The stored predicted ranks are used to reproduce the original
quintile assignments,

\[
Q_i=1+\left\lfloor\frac{\widehat R_i-1}{39}\right\rfloor.
\]

Average ranks can produce unequal groups if a tie crosses a
quintile boundary. Consequently, the next block also compares
the rank-based assignments with the positions obtained by
ordering GEBV in decreasing order and ID as the secondary
criterion. The historical allocation is retained because the
stored predicted ranks are untied and both assignments coincide.
The observed BLUP ranks can contain ties; they are not used to
construct these GEBV quintiles.

```{r pairwise-quintile-weighted-kappa}
# Reproduce the original GEBV quintile assignments.
all_ranking$GEBV_Quintile <- (
  (
    all_ranking$GEBV_Rank - 1L
  ) %/%
    39L
) + 1L

quintile_counts <- data.frame()
quintile_diagnostics <- data.frame()

for (trait in traits) {
  for (model_name in model_order) {
    quintile_data <- all_ranking[
      all_ranking$Trait == trait & all_ranking$Model == model_name,
      , drop = FALSE
    ]
    counts <- table(factor(quintile_data$GEBV_Quintile, levels = 1:5))
    position_order <- order(-quintile_data$GEBV, quintile_data$ID)
    position_quintile <- integer(nrow(quintile_data))
    position_quintile[position_order] <- (seq_len(nrow(quintile_data)) - 1L) %/% 39L + 1L

    quintile_counts <- rbind(quintile_counts, data.frame(
      Trait = trait, Model = model_name,
      Quintile = 1:5, Individuals = as.integer(counts),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    ))
    quintile_diagnostics <- rbind(quintile_diagnostics, data.frame(
      Trait = trait, Model = model_name,
      Tied_rank_records = sum(duplicated(quintile_data$GEBV_Rank) |
        duplicated(quintile_data$GEBV_Rank, fromLast = TRUE)),
      Q1 = as.integer(counts[1]), Q2 = as.integer(counts[2]),
      Q3 = as.integer(counts[3]), Q4 = as.integer(counts[4]),
      Q5 = as.integer(counts[5]),
      Position_disagreements = sum(quintile_data$GEBV_Quintile != position_quintile),
      Top20_disagreements = sum((quintile_data$GEBV_Quintile == 1L) != quintile_data$GEBV_Top20),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    ))
  }
}

```

The table displays the five group sizes, tied predicted rank records,
disagreements with the position-based allocation and disagreements
between quintile 1 and the stored predicted upper group.

```{r display-quintile-diagnostics}
knitr::kable(
  quintile_diagnostics, format = "html", row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "GEBV quintile sizes and agreement with ordered positions and top-20% membership",
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "100%")
```

### 6.6 Linearly weighted Cohen's kappa

For quintiles \(a,b\in\{1,\ldots,5\}\), the linear weight is

\[
w_{ab}=1-\frac{|a-b|}{4}.
\]

Linear weights decrease from one for identical quintiles to zero
for quintiles four categories apart. The matrix `quintile_weights`
assigns these values to all 25 pairs of quintile categories.

```{r compute-linear-quintile-weights}
quintile_levels <- seq_len(5L)

quintile_weights <- matrix(0, nrow = 5L, ncol = 5L)

for (row_index in quintile_levels) {

  for (column_index in quintile_levels) {

    quintile_weights[row_index, column_index] <- 1 - abs(
        row_index - column_index
      ) / 4
  }
}

```

Let \(n_{ab}\) be the number of matched individuals classified
in quintile \(a\) by one model and quintile \(b\) by the other.
With \(n=195\), define \(p_{ab}=n_{ab}/n\) and marginal
proportions \(p_{a+}\) and \(p_{+b}\). The observed and
independence-based expected weighted agreements are

\[
P_o^w=\sum_{a=1}^{5}\sum_{b=1}^{5}w_{ab}p_{ab},
\qquad
P_e^w=\sum_{a=1}^{5}\sum_{b=1}^{5}w_{ab}p_{a+}p_{+b}.
\]

The coefficient is

\[
\kappa_w=\frac{P_o^w-P_e^w}{1-P_e^w}.
\]

A value of one indicates perfect agreement, zero indicates the
weighted agreement expected under independence, and negative
values indicate agreement below that reference. Two complementary
descriptive statistics are the exact agreement rate and mean
absolute quintile difference:

\[
A=\sum_{a=1}^{5}p_{aa},\qquad
D_Q=\sum_{a=1}^{5}\sum_{b=1}^{5}|a-b|p_{ab}.
\]

The comparisons pair individuals explicitly by ID, rather than
assuming that separate sorts necessarily represent the same
population. The expected ID set, uniqueness and completeness of
both models are examined for each pair. An invalid or incomplete
pair has undefined agreement statistics rather than an estimate
based on mismatched individuals. All 21 pairs per trait are
retained in `kappa_summary`.

```{r compare-ranking-quintiles}
# Compare every pair of genomic models separately within each trait.
pairwise_id_coverage <- data.frame()
kappa_summary <- data.frame(
  Trait = character(0),
  Model_1 = character(0),
  Model_2 = character(0),
  Weighted_Kappa = numeric(0),
  Exact_Quintile_Agreement_Rate = numeric(0),
  Mean_Absolute_Quintile_Difference = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (trait in traits) {

  for (model_1_index in seq_len(length(model_order) - 1L)) {

    for (model_2_index in seq(from = model_1_index + 1L, to = length(model_order))) {

      model_1 <- model_order[model_1_index]

      model_2 <- model_order[model_2_index]

      x <- all_ranking[
        all_ranking$Trait == trait & all_ranking$Model == model_1,
        c("ID", "GEBV_Quintile"),
        drop = FALSE
      ]

      y <- all_ranking[
        all_ranking$Trait == trait & all_ranking$Model == model_2,
        c("ID", "GEBV_Quintile"),
        drop = FALSE
      ]

      complete_pair <- !anyNA(x$ID) && !anyNA(y$ID) &&
        !anyDuplicated(x$ID) && !anyDuplicated(y$ID) &&
        setequal(x$ID, ranking_expected_ids) &&
        setequal(y$ID, ranking_expected_ids) &&
        all(x$GEBV_Quintile %in% quintile_levels) &&
        all(y$GEBV_Quintile %in% quintile_levels)

      pairwise_id_coverage <- rbind(pairwise_id_coverage, data.frame(
        Trait = trait, Model_1 = model_1, Model_2 = model_2,
        Matched_IDs = length(intersect(x$ID, y$ID)),
        Complete_pair = complete_pair,
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      ))

      x <- x[order(x$ID),, drop = FALSE]
      y <- y[match(x$ID, y$ID),, drop = FALSE]

      weighted_kappa <- exact_quintile_agreement_rate <-
        mean_absolute_quintile_difference <- NA_real_

      if (complete_pair) {
        agreement_table <- table(
          factor(x$GEBV_Quintile, levels = quintile_levels),
          factor(y$GEBV_Quintile, levels = quintile_levels)
        )

        observed_proportion <- agreement_table / sum(agreement_table)

        row_marginal <- rowSums(observed_proportion)

        column_marginal <- colSums(observed_proportion)

        expected_proportion <- outer(row_marginal, column_marginal)

        observed_weighted_agreement <- sum(quintile_weights * observed_proportion)

        expected_weighted_agreement <- sum(quintile_weights * expected_proportion)

        weighted_kappa <- (
            observed_weighted_agreement - expected_weighted_agreement
          ) / (1 - expected_weighted_agreement)

        exact_quintile_agreement_rate <- mean(x$GEBV_Quintile == y$GEBV_Quintile)

        mean_absolute_quintile_difference <- mean(abs(x$GEBV_Quintile - y$GEBV_Quintile))
      }

      kappa_summary <- rbind(
        kappa_summary,
        data.frame(
          Trait = trait,
          Model_1 = model_1,
          Model_2 = model_2,
          Weighted_Kappa = weighted_kappa,
          Exact_Quintile_Agreement_Rate = exact_quintile_agreement_rate,
          Mean_Absolute_Quintile_Difference = mean_absolute_quintile_difference,
          stringsAsFactors = FALSE
        )
      )
    }
  }
}

KAPPA_SUMMARY_CSV <- file.path(COMPARISON_DIR, "real_model_pairwise_quintile_weighted_kappa.csv")

kappa_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Linearly weighted Cohen's kappa for each pair of genomic methods based on GEBV-ranking quintiles",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
  ) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "100%")
```

The matching summary reports how many of the 21 pairs per trait
have the complete R03 population and valid quintile assignments.

```{r display-pairwise-id-coverage}
pairwise_coverage_summary <- data.frame()

for (trait in traits) {
  pair_data <- pairwise_id_coverage[pairwise_id_coverage$Trait == trait, , drop = FALSE]
  pairwise_coverage_summary <- rbind(pairwise_coverage_summary, data.frame(
    Trait = trait,
    Pairs = nrow(pair_data),
    Complete_pairs = sum(pair_data$Complete_pair),
    Min_matched_IDs = min(pair_data$Matched_IDs),
    Max_matched_IDs = max(pair_data$Matched_IDs),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ))
}

knitr::kable(
  pairwise_coverage_summary, format = "html", row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Completeness of individual pairing for quintile agreement",
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
)
```

The coefficient describes agreement between genomic models, not
agreement with observed BLUPs or predictive superiority.
The 63 coefficients are not independent because they reuse the
same individuals and models. In the stored results, agreement
between GBLUP_AD and GBLUP_ADE is particularly high; the largest
disagreements occur between some GBLUP and ANN pairs, especially
for LP. Identical or similar quintile classifications need not
imply identical predicted values or rank positions.

```

The heatmap displays each of the 21 unordered pairs twice in
a symmetric matrix, with self-agreement on the diagonal.
The three traits are shown separately.

```{r pairwise-quintile-weighted-kappa-heatmap, fig.width=13, fig.height=8.5, fig.alt="Three annotated symmetric seven by seven model-pair kappa matrices.", fig.cap="Linearly weighted Cohen's kappa for every pair of the seven genomic methods based on GEBV-ranking quintiles. Each panel is a complete 7 by 7 pairwise matrix for one trait; no aggregation by model family is applied. Larger values indicate stronger agreement in selection strata."}
kappa_heatmap <- data.frame(
  Trait = character(0),
  Model_1 = character(0),
  Model_2 = character(0),
  Weighted_Kappa = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (trait in traits) {

  for (model_1 in model_order) {

    for (model_2 in model_order) {

      if (model_1 == model_2) {

        kappa_value <- 1

      } else {

        pair_row <- kappa_summary[
          kappa_summary$Trait == trait & (
              (
                kappa_summary$Model_1 == model_1 & kappa_summary$Model_2 == model_2
              ) | (kappa_summary$Model_1 == model_2 & kappa_summary$Model_2 == model_1)
            ),
          ,
          drop = FALSE
        ]

        kappa_value <- pair_row$Weighted_Kappa
      }

      kappa_heatmap <- rbind(
        kappa_heatmap,
        data.frame(
          Trait = trait,
          Model_1 = model_1,
          Model_2 = model_2,
          Weighted_Kappa = kappa_value,
          stringsAsFactors = FALSE
        )
      )
    }
  }
}

kappa_heatmap$Model_1 <- factor(kappa_heatmap$Model_1, levels = model_order, labels = model_labels)

kappa_heatmap$Model_2 <- factor(kappa_heatmap$Model_2, levels = rev(model_order), labels = rev(model_labels))

kappa_heatmap$Trait <- factor(kappa_heatmap$Trait, levels = traits)

kappa_heatmap$Text_color <- ifelse(abs(kappa_heatmap$Weighted_Kappa) >= 0.65, "white", "black")

p_kappa <- ggplot(
  kappa_heatmap,
  aes(x = Model_1, y = Model_2, fill = Weighted_Kappa)
) + geom_tile(
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) + geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Weighted_Kappa), color = Text_color),
    size = 3.2,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) + scale_color_identity() + scale_fill_gradient2(
    name = "Weighted kappa",
    low = "#B2182B",
    mid = "#F7F7F7",
    high = "#2166AC",
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-1, 1)
  ) + facet_wrap(
    ~ Trait,
    nrow = 1
  ) + coord_fixed() + labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) + theme_gdocs() + theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

print(p_kappa)
```
