as the global ranking. Each trait is displayed separately, with
identical limits for observed and predicted values across the
seven models, and equal physical units on both axes. The dashed

makes differences in predicted dispersion visible, without
compressing Cer or BM into the wider LP range.

## 8. Integrated interpretation

### 8.1 Cer

GBLUP_A gives the highest common-split mean Pearson (0.6303)
and Spearman (0.6297), and the smallest mean RMSE (0.1615).
The matched contrasts favor GBLUP for every ANN–GBLUP pair
and primary metric. The three GBLUP structures differ little
in predictive performance for this trait.

GBLUP_A also has the highest global Spearman (0.6425) and the
smallest mean absolute rank error (36.40 positions). All three
GBLUP structures recover 22 of the 39 observed upper-group
individuals. ANN_L1_L2 gives the highest global Spearman among
the ANN variants (0.6145), while ANN_L1 recovers the most
upper-group individuals among the ANNs (20 of 39).

GBLUP_AD and GBLUP_ADE have identical quintile assignments
(weighted kappa 1). The lowest kappa (0.7821) is shared by
GBLUP_AD versus ANN_0 and GBLUP_ADE versus ANN_0.

### 8.2 BM

GBLUP_A gives the highest common-split Pearson (0.3062) and
Spearman (0.2607) and the smallest RMSE (0.1445);
GBLUP_AD gives the smallest MAE (0.1190). All matched mean
contrasts favor GBLUP, although the differences are smaller
than for Cer in correlation units.

Individual ordering gives a different result: ANN_0 has the
highest global Spearman (0.2686), the smallest mean absolute
rank error (54.24 positions) and the greatest upper-group
recovery (12 of 39). These descriptive differences do not
imply reliable selection of every individual. The highest kappa
is 0.9615 (GBLUP_AD versus GBLUP_ADE) and the lowest is
0.6603 (GBLUP_A versus ANN_L2).

### 8.3 LP

GBLUP_A gives the highest mean Pearson (0.2073) and Spearman
(0.2137) on the 23 common finite splits. It also gives the
smallest RMSE (1.2385) and MAE (0.9756) on all 25 splits.
The four constant-prediction GBLUP assessments remain part of
the error evaluation.

Six matched correlation contrasts favor an ANN when compared
with GBLUP_AD or GBLUP_ADE on 24 finite splits. All matched
error contrasts favor GBLUP. These comparisons refer to different
finite subsets and do not conflict with the seven-model ordering.

After OOF aggregation, ANN_L2 gives the highest global Spearman
(0.2308) and the smallest mean absolute rank error (54.27
positions), while ANN_L1_L2 recovers the most upper-group
individuals (13 of 39). Weighted kappa ranges from 0.4359
(GBLUP_A versus ANN_L2) to 0.9872 (GBLUP_AD versus GBLUP_ADE),
illustrating differences between model-specific selection strata.

### 8.4 Explicit weight regularization

The ANN variants are compared within each trait using ANN_0 as
the reference without explicit L1 or L2 weight penalties.
All variants use early stopping in the selection of training
duration, and their hyperparameters were tuned separately within
the outer analysis samples. Differences are therefore comparisons
of the fitted procedures, not isolated causal effects of penalties.

| Trait | Highest ANN common-split Pearson | Highest ANN common-split Spearman | Smallest ANN RMSE | Smallest ANN MAE | Highest ANN global Spearman | Largest ANN upper-group recovery |
|:------|:---------------------------------|:----------------------------------|:------------------|:-----------------|:----------------------------|:--------------------------------|
| Cer | ANN_L1_L2 | ANN_L1_L2 | ANN_L1_L2 | ANN_L1_L2 | ANN_L1_L2 | ANN_L1 |
| BM | ANN_L1_L2 | ANN_0 | ANN_L1_L2 | ANN_L2 | ANN_0 | ANN_0 |
| LP | ANN_L2 | ANN_L2 | ANN_L1 | ANN_L1 | ANN_L2 | ANN_L1_L2 |

For Cer, combining L1 and L2 gives favorable mean association
and error relative to ANN_0, although L1 alone recovers more
upper-group individuals. For BM, the combined penalty gives
the highest ANN Pearson and lowest RMSE, but ANN_0 gives
better global ordering and upper-group recovery. For LP, L2
gives stronger correlation and global ordering, while L1 gives
the smallest mean errors among the ANNs. The combined penalty
gives the largest upper-group recovery.

The calibration results complement these comparisons. GBLUP
has the smallest absolute mean bias for each trait, whereas
ANN_L1 (Cer and LP) and ANN_L1_L2 (BM) have mean slopes
closest to one. In LP, the GBLUP slopes are highly variable
and exclude constant-prediction splits. A mean slope close to
one alone does not establish reliable prediction or calibration
on every split.

### 8.5 Conclusions and limitations

The seven procedures share the same outer assessment individuals
and the same observed BLUPs. GBLUP_A provides the highest
descriptive common-split association in all three traits and
the smallest mean RMSE. The ranking and recovery criteria
favor different procedures for BM and LP. This is compatible
with the fact that averaging repeated OOF predictions changes
the unit of evaluation from held-out splits to individuals.

The three GBLUP structures produce highly similar quintile
assignments. Agreement is reported separately for each of
the 21 unordered model pairs within each trait; no family-level
kappa average is calculated. High agreement does not establish
predictive validity.

The comparison is against precomputed phenotypic BLUPs rather
than known true genetic values. Repeated cross-validation
reuses individuals, and neither split-level variability nor
matched mean differences are interpreted as independent-replicate
inference. The sample contains 195 individuals and the conclusions
are conditional on these data and the fitted procedures.
Upper-group recovery is based on descending BLUPs, not
necessarily the favorable selection direction for each trait,
and cannot be interpreted as realized genetic gain.

## 9. Numerical outputs, figures and navigation

### 9.1 Numerical summaries

The seven CSV files in `output/real/comparison/` contain the
comparison summaries shown in the tutorial. The six unchanged
summaries retain their existing exports; the ranking-winners CSV
is written by the code in Section 6.3 so that tied optima are
represented in the saved result as well as in the HTML.
No model fitting or modification of the upstream R04A and R04B
outputs is required.

```{r comparison-output-inventory}
comparison_output_inventory <- data.frame(
  File = basename(c(
    PERFORMANCE_SUMMARY_CSV, COMMON_CORRELATION_SUMMARY_CSV,
    PREDICTIVE_WINNERS_CSV, PAIRED_SUMMARY_CSV,
    RANKING_SUMMARY_CSV, RANKING_WINNERS_CSV, KAPPA_SUMMARY_CSV
  )),
  Records = c(
    nrow(performance_summary), nrow(common_correlation_summary),
    nrow(predictive_winners), nrow(paired_summary),
    nrow(ranking_summary), nrow(ranking_winners), nrow(kappa_summary)
  ),
  Unit = c(
    "Trait and model", "Trait and model", "Trait",
    "Trait and ANN-GBLUP pair", "Trait and model", "Trait",
    "Trait and unordered model pair"
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  comparison_output_inventory, format = "html", row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Numerical summaries of the seven-model comparison",
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "100%")
```
